analysis.one_liner: Requires side underride guards on new large trucks and trailers so cars and people can't slide underneath in crashes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, the bill has drawn nine Democratic cosponsors but no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: When a car, motorcycle, or bicycle hits a large truck, it can slide underneath the trailer — an 'underride' crash that shears off the top of the car or leaves a rider under the truck. The bill would order the Transportation Department to write rules requiring side underride guards on new trailers, semitrailers, and single-unit trucks within 18 months, with full compliance two years later. It would also reconvene a federal advisory committee on underride protection, publish all underride research on a public website, commission studies by the National Academies and the Government Accountability Office, review how crashes are reported in the federal fatality database, and create free online training for police on how to identify underride crashes.
analysis.who_benefits: People driving cars, riding motorcycles, or walking or cycling near large trucks. The bill's own findings cite over 31,500 deaths in underride crashes since the 1970s and note that a federal advisory committee concluded no substantial progress has been made to prevent them. Side guards are designed to keep a striking vehicle's occupant compartment intact at crash speeds up to 40 mph and to stop people from sliding under the side of a trailer.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Transportation Secretary to finalize safety standards within 18 months of enactment mandating side underride guards on new trailers, semitrailers, and single-unit trucks, with full compliance required two years after the rules are finalized.

The required standard must prevent intrusion into a car's occupant survival space in perpendicular crashes at speeds up to 40 mph and must impede vulnerable road users from passing under the side of a truck.

The bill's findings cite the federal Advisory Committee on Underride Protection's count of 25,100 underride crashes and 31,500 corresponding fatalities since the creation of the highway safety agency, and its conclusion that no substantial progress has been made by the Transportation Department to prevent them.

The bill also requires the reconvening of the federal Advisory Committee on Underride Protection, a public website publishing all underride research and victim stories, a National Academies study on front-override crashes, a GAO study of the 2022 rear-guard rule, a review of how underride crashes are counted in the federal fatality database, and free web-based training for state and local police on documenting underride crashes.
The required guards must contribute to fuel efficiency through aerodynamic design, and the mandated cost-benefit analysis must count net fuel savings against voluntary side skirts already in use.

analysis.who_pays: Trailer and truck manufacturers, and ultimately freight carriers and shipping customers, bear the cost of equipping every new trailer, semitrailer, and single-unit truck with side underride guards. The bill requires the government to weigh those costs in its cost-benefit analysis, alongside counted fuel savings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Trailer makers, trucking fleets, freight customers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds an upfront equipment cost to every new trailer, semitrailer, and single-unit truck, a cost that freight carriers would likely pass through to shipping prices — the bill requires the Secretary to calculate costs and benefits before finalizing the rules.
The mandate applies only to new vehicles, so the existing truck fleet turns over slowly and the safety benefits would phase in over many years rather than immediately.

The bill does not leave the decision to the safety agency: it sets a deadline, fixes the performance standard, and dictates what the cost-benefit analysis must include, including a specific method for counting net fuel savings — a good-faith objection is that Congress is substituting its judgment for the agency's on a technically complex rulemaking, one that the agency itself had only explored through an early-stage notice in April 2023 that the bill anticipates may be withdrawn.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose — keeping car occupants and vulnerable road users from dying in slide-under crashes — is a straightforward safety gain, and the bill tries to offset the equipment cost by requiring aerodynamic design and counting fuel savings. The honest tradeoffs are the added cost per new trailer passed into freight prices, the slow phase-in because only new vehicles are covered, and Congress pre-writing a technical rulemaking that the safety agency had not yet decided to pursue. On balance, the benefits to crash survivors run to the public; the costs run to manufacturers and freight customers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on its first day and has sat there since, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on February 4, 2026, with five original cosponsors — Senators Lujan, Blumenthal, Van Hollen, Duckworth, and Warren — and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
A total of nine Democratic senators have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has.

The bill's findings cite the Advisory Committee on Underride Protection's report of 25,100 underrides and 31,500 corresponding fatalities, and its conclusion that no substantial progress has been made by the Department of Transportation to prevent these crash fatalities.

The bill is written to work even if the Transportation Secretary withdraws the agency's April 2023 advance notice of proposed rulemaking on side underride guards, stating that any such withdrawal would not affect the requirement to finalize regulations.
Since the February 2026 referral, the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trailer and truck manufacturers, and the freight industry generally, are better off so far, because the bill has not moved and the equipment mandate has not advanced. The federal safety agency also retains the status quo, in which side underride guards remain a matter it explored but did not require.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trailer and truck manufacturers, for now

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican senator has.

for.name: Families of underride crash victims and underride safety advocates
for.what_they_did: Have campaigned for years for comprehensive underride guard mandates; the bill's findings section is written in memory of dozens of named victims, and its advisory-committee provisions add seats for families of crash victims.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote — in the months since.

against.name: Trucking and trailer manufacturing industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed mandatory underride guard requirements as costly equipment mandates; no opposition from them to this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken yet, but all nine cosponsors are Democrats among the 45-member Democratic caucus and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: The bill would require side underride guards on every new trailer and semitrailer within two years of the rules being finalized, adding equipment cost per unit. The cost is the price of a safety feature that protects people in crashes with those trailers.
Carriers would buy compliant new equipment as their fleets turn over and could pass those costs into shipping prices. The bill counts fuel savings from aerodynamic guard design as a partial offset.

industries.industry: Aerodynamic equipment and side skirt makers
industries.note: Because the required guards must integrate aerodynamic, fuel-saving design, makers of side skirts and similar equipment would supply the mandated hardware. The bill's cost-benefit rules account for fuel savings relative to voluntary side skirt adoption.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support and months of committee inaction, the bill is unlikely to get a standalone hearing or vote this Congress. Its most realistic path is being folded into the next surface transportation reauthorization, where safety mandates have historically been negotiated; similar versions of the Stop Underrides Act introduced in earlier congresses also died in committee without a vote.
